nodes.name: Parseval frame not unitarily equivalent to an orthonormal basis
nodes.statement: For example, let $X=[0,d)$ under Lesbesgue measure, where $d$ is the dimension of $H$ and may be infinite, and let $\left\{ h_{k}\right\} _{k=0}^{d-1}$ be an orthonormal basis for $H.$ Then the $H$ valued function $$ F\left( x\right) =e^{i2\pi x}\ h_{_{\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor }}, $$ where $\left\lfloor \; \right\rfloor $ is the floor function, is a frame on $H$. Any unitary operator $U$ such that $$ U\left[ F\left( x\right) \right] = h_{\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor } $$ would necessarily imply $U\left[ F\left( k\right) \right] =h_{k},$ thus implying that $U=I.$ However, $$U\left[ F\left( k+\frac{1}{2}\right) \right] =-h_{k}$$ implies that $U\neq I,$ and consequently, $F\left( x\right) $ is not unitarily equivalent to $\left\{ h_{k}\right\} .$
nodes.statement_short: On $X=[0,d)$, $F(x)=e^{i2\pi x}h_{\lfloor x\rfloor}$ is a Parseval frame not unitarily equivalent to the basis $\{h_k\}$.

nodes.name: Parseval frame from two orthonormal bases
nodes.statement: For example, if both $\left\{ f_{k}\right\} _{k=0}^{d-1}$ and $\left\{ h_{k}\right\} _{k=0}^{d-1}$ are orthonormal bases of $H,$ and if we define $$ F\left( x\right) =\cos \left( 2\pi x\right) f_{\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor}+i\sin \left( 2\pi x\right) h_{\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor }, $$ then for any $\phi \in H,$ we notice that $$ \int_{0}^{d}\left\vert \left\langle \phi ,F\left( x\right) \right\rangle \right\vert ^{2}dx=\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\int_{k}^{k+1}\left\vert \left\langle \phi ,F\left( x\right) \right\rangle \right\vert ^{2}dx=\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\int_{0}^{1}\left\vert \left\langle \phi ,F\left( \xi +k\right) \right\rangle \right\vert ^{2}d\xi $$ and $F\left( \xi +k\right) =\cos \left( 2\pi \xi \right) f_{k}+i\sin \left(2\pi \xi \right) h_{k},$ from which it follows that $F\left( x\right) $ is also a Parseval frame.
nodes.statement_short: $F(x)=\cos(2\pi x)f_{\lfloor x\rfloor}+i\sin(2\pi x)h_{\lfloor x\rfloor}$ built from two orthonormal bases is a Parseval frame.

nodes.name: Parseval frame on a product space from two Parseval frames
nodes.statement: Moreover, if $F\left( x\right) $ and $G\left(x\right) $ are both Parseval frames over $H,$ then define $$ K\left( x,y\right) = \cos \left( 2\pi y\right) F\left( x\right) +i\sin \left( 2\pi y\right) G\left( x\right) $$ for $y$ in $[0,1].$ The same approach as above shows that $K\left(x,y\right)$ over $X\times Y$ is also a Parseval frame, and in fact, the same approach leads to the following proposition:
nodes.statement_short: $K(x,y)=\cos(2\pi y)F(x)+i\sin(2\pi y)G(x)$ is a Parseval frame over $X\times Y$.

nodes.name: Parseval frames combined via an orthonormal subset of L^2
nodes.statement: If $F_{j}\left( x\right) $, $j\in \mathbb{Z}$, are Parseval frames from a measure space $\left( X,\mu \right) $ into a separable Hilbert space $H,$ and if $\alpha _{j}\left( y\right) ,\ \ j\in \mathbb{Z}$, is an orthonormal subset of $L^{2}\left( Y,\nu \right) $ for a measure space $\left( Y,\nu \right) ,$ then $$ K\left( x,y\right) =\sum_{j=-\infty }^{\infty }\alpha _{j}\left( y\right) F_{j}\left( x\right) $$ is a Parseval frame on $H$ over the product measure space of $X$ and $Y.$
nodes.statement_short: A sum $\sum_j\alpha_j(y)F_j(x)$ of Parseval frames weighted by an orthonormal family in $L^2(Y,\nu)$ is a Parseval frame on $X\times Y$.
assumptions: $F_{j}\left( x\right) $, $j\in \mathbb{Z}$, are Parseval frames from a measure space $\left( X,\mu \right) $ into a separable Hilbert space $H,$
$\alpha _{j}\left( y\right) ,\ \ j\in \mathbb{Z}$, is an orthonormal subset of $L^{2}\left( Y,\nu \right) $ for a measure space $\left( Y,\nu \right) ,$

nodes.name: Matrix of a finite frame
nodes.statement: Given $\left\{ f_{1},\ldots ,f_{n}\right\} \subset \mathbb{C}^{m},$ we form the matrix $$ T=\left[ \begin{array}{c} f_{1}^{\ast } \\ \vdots \\ f_{n}^{\ast } \end{array} \right] $$ where $f_{j}^{\ast }$ is the Hermitian transpose of the column vector $f_{j}.$
nodes.statement_short: For vectors $f_1,\dots,f_n\in\mathbb{C}^m$, $T$ is the $n\times m$ matrix whose rows are $f_j^*$.

nodes.name: Singular value decomposition
nodes.statement: The singular value decomposition of $T$ is given by $$ T=U\tilde{\Sigma}V^{\ast }\ \ where\ \ \tilde{\Sigma}= \left[ \begin{array}{c} \Sigma \\ 0 \end{array} \right] $$ with $\Sigma =diag\left( s_{1},\ldots ,s_{m}\right);$ where $s_{1}\geq \ldots \geq s_{m}\geq 0$ are the singular values of $T;$ where $U:\mathbb{C}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb{C}^{n}$ is unitary; and where $V:\mathbb{C}^{m}\mapsto \mathbb{C}^{m}$ is also unitary.
nodes.statement_short: $T=U\tilde\Sigma V^*$ with $\Sigma$ the diagonal of singular values and $U,V$ unitary.
conclusions: $$ T=U\tilde{\Sigma}V^{\ast }\ \ where\ \ \tilde{\Sigma}= \left[ \begin{array}{c} \Sigma \\ 0 \end{array} \right] $$

nodes.name: Proof of singular-value frame bounds
nodes.statement: For any $\phi \in \mathbb{C}^{m},$ it follows that $$ \left\Vert T\phi \right\Vert ^{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left\vert \left\langle \phi, f_{k}\right\rangle \right\vert ^{2} $$ and from the properties of the singular value decomposition, $$s_{m}^{2}\left\Vert \phi \right\Vert ^{2}\leq \left\Vert T\phi \right\Vert^{2}\leq s_{1}^{2}\ \left\Vert \phi \right\Vert ^{2}$$
nodes.statement_short: Direct: $\|T\phi\|^2$ equals the frame sum, and the SVD bounds it between $s_m^2\|\phi\|^2$ and $s_1^2\|\phi\|^2$.

nodes.name: Frame bounds from singular values
nodes.statement: If $s_{m}>0,$ then $\left\{ f_{1},\ldots ,f_{n}\right\} $ is a frame on $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ with frame bounds $A=s_{m}^{2}$ and $B=s_{1}^{2}$ \cite{casazza2013introduction,aldroubi2007optimal}.
nodes.statement_short: If the smallest singular value $s_m>0$, the vectors form a frame with bounds $s_m^2$ and $s_1^2$.
conclusions: $\left\{ f_{1},\ldots ,f_{n}\right\} $ is a frame on $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ with frame bounds $A=s_{m}^{2}$ and $B=s_{1}^{2}$

nodes.statement: If we define $$g_{j}=S^{-1/2}f_{j}$$ then $\left\{ g_{1},\ldots ,g_{n}\right\} $ is a \emph{Parseval frame} in $\mathbb{C}^{m},$ and in fact, if we define $$ T_{p}=\left[ \begin{array}{c} g_{1}^{\ast } \\ \vdots \\ g_{n}^{\ast } \end{array} \right] $$ then the singular value decomposition of $T_{p}$ is $$ T_{p}=U\left[ \begin{array}{c} I_{m} \\ 0 \end{array} \right] V^{\ast } $$ where $U,V$ are the same as for $T$ and $I_{m}$ is the $m\times m$ identity matrix.

nodes.name: Frame bounds and Parseval frame
nodes.statement: The constants $A,B$ are called the \emph{frame bounds} of $f$, and if $A=B=1,$ then $f$ is called a \emph{Parseval frame}. Specifically, a Parseval frame $f$ satisfies $$\int_{X}\left\vert \left\langle \phi,f\left( x\right) \right\rangle \right\vert ^{2}d\mu \left( x\right) = \left\Vert \phi \right\Vert ^{2} $$ for all $\phi \in H$.
nodes.statement_short: $A,B$ are the frame bounds; $f$ is Parseval when $A=B=1$, i.e. $\int_X|\langle\phi,f(x)\rangle|^2d\mu=\|\phi\|^2$.

nodes.name: Analysis, synthesis and frame operators
nodes.statement: Let $f:X\mapsto H$ be a frame. The operator defined by \begin{equation} V:H\mapsto L^2(X), \quad (V\phi)(x) = \brak{\phi, f(x)}_H \tag{Analysis Operator} \end{equation} is well-defined, bounded, and has a bounded inverse. The adjoint of $V$ is given by \begin{equation} V^*:L^2(X)\mapsto H, \quad V^*\alpha = \int_X \alpha(x)f(x)\,d\mu(x), \tag{Synthesis Operator} \end{equation} where convergence of the integral is taken in $H$. Finally, the operator defined by \begin{equation} S:H\mapsto H, \quad S\phi = V^*V\phi = \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x) \tag{Frame Operator} \end{equation} is positive, self-adjoint, bounded, and has a bounded inverse.
nodes.statement_short: A frame's analysis operator $V$ is bounded with bounded inverse; its adjoint is the synthesis integral, and $S=V^*V$ is positive, self-adjoint and invertible.
conclusions: is well-defined, bounded, and has a bounded inverse.

nodes.name: Existence of a dual frame
nodes.statement: Let $f:X\mapsto H$ be a frame. Then, there exists a frame $\tilde{f}:X\mapsto H$ such that for all $\phi\in H$, \begin{equation} \phi = \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)} \tilde{f}(x)\,d\mu(x). \tag{Reconstruction Property} \end{equation} Any such $\tilde{f}$ is called a \emph{dual frame} of $f$. Moreover, if $f$ is the frame operator of $f$, then the map $\tilde{f}:X\mapsto H$ defined by $\tilde{f}(x)=S^{-1}f(x)$ is a dual frame of $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Every frame has a dual frame giving the reconstruction formula; $S^{-1}f$ is one.

nodes.name: GL(H)
nodes.statement: Let $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ be the group of all invertible bounded linear operators on $H$ with bounded inverse.

nodes.name: GL^+(H)
nodes.statement: Let $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)\subset \operatorname{GL}(H)$ be the cone of all positive operators in $\operatorname{GL}(H)$.

nodes.name: Adjugation
nodes.statement: For every $A\in \operatorname{GL}(H)$, let the map $\operatorname{ad}_A:\operatorname{GL}(H)\mapsto \operatorname{GL}(H)$ be defined $$\operatorname{ad}_A(B) = ABA^*.$$ We say that $\operatorname{ad}_A(B)$ is the \emph{adjugation} of $B$ by $A$.

nodes.name: Adjugation relation ~
nodes.statement: We define the relation $\sim$ on $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ by $B\sim B^\prime$ if and only if $\operatorname{ad}_A(B)=B^\prime$ for some $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$.

nodes.name: Adjugation is an equivalence relation
nodes.statement: The relation $\sim$ is an equivalence relation.
conclusions: The relation $\sim$ is an equivalence relation.

nodes.name: Proof that ~ is an equivalence relation
nodes.statement: Let $B\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Clearly, $\operatorname{ad}_I(B)=IBI^*=B$, so that $B\sim B$. Thus, $\sim$ is reflexive. Given $B,B^\prime\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$, suppose $B\sim B^\prime$. That is, $ad_A(B)=ABA*=B^\prime$ for some $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Then, \[ \operatorname{ad}_{A^{-1}}(B^\prime) = A^{-1}B^\prime (A^{-1})^* = A^{-1}ABA^*(A^*)^{-1} = B. \] Thus, $B^\prime\sim B$, and hence $\sim$ is symmetric. Finally, suppose $B\sim B^\prime$ and $B^\prime\sim B^{\prime\prime}$. Thus, $\operatorname{ad}_A(B)=ABA^*=B^\prime$ and $\operatorname{ad}_{A^\prime}(B^\prime)=A^\prime B^\prime (A^\prime)^*=B^{\prime\prime}$ for some $A,A^\prime\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Then, \[ \operatorname{ad}_{A^\prime A}(B) = A^\prime AB(A^\prime A)^* = A^\prime (ABA^*)(A^\prime)^* = A^\prime B^\prime (A^\prime)^* = B^{\prime\prime}. \] Thus, $B\sim B^{\prime\prime}$, and hence $\sim$ is transitive.
nodes.statement_short: Check reflexivity with $\operatorname{ad}_I$, symmetry with $\operatorname{ad}_{A^{-1}}$, transitivity with $\operatorname{ad}_{A'A}$.

nodes.name: Adjugacy classes
nodes.statement: The equivalence classes in $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ induced by $\sim$ are called \emph{adjugacy classes}.

nodes.name: GL^+(H) is an adjugacy class
nodes.statement: The space $GL^+(H)$ is an adjugacy class in $\operatorname{GL}(H)$.
conclusions: The space $GL^+(H)$ is an adjugacy class in $\operatorname{GL}(H)$.

nodes.name: Proof that GL^+(H) is an adjugacy class
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$ and $B\in\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$. For any $\phi\in H$, we have \[ \brak{\operatorname{ad}_A(B)\phi, \phi} = \brak{ABA^*\phi, \phi} = \brak{BA^*\phi, A^*\phi}\geq 0, \] where the inequality holds since $A^*\phi\in H$ and $B$ is positive. Thus, $\operatorname{ad}_A(B)$ is positive, so that $GL^+(H)$ is closed under adjugation. Let $B,C\in\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$. Since $B,C$ are positive, then $B=SS^*$ and $C=TT^*$ for some $S,T\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. There exists $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$ such that $T=AS$. We have \[ \operatorname{ad}_A(B) = ABA^* = ASS^*A^* = (AS)(AS)^* = TT^* = C. \] Thus, $B\sim C$. Ergo, $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ is an adjugacy class.
nodes.statement_short: Adjugation preserves positivity; any two positive $B=SS^*$, $C=TT^*$ are related by $\operatorname{ad}_A$ with $T=AS$.

nodes.name: Projection rho(A)=AA*
nodes.statement: Next, we define the projection \begin{equation} \rho:\operatorname{GL}(H)\mapsto \operatorname{GL}^+(H), \quad \rho(A)=AA^*, \end{equation} which is important in the proof of the following lemma establishing an important relationship between $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ and $\operatorname{GL}(H)$.

nodes.name: Definition of rho
nodes.statement: \rho:\operatorname{GL}(H)\mapsto \operatorname{GL}^+(H), \quad \rho(A)=AA^*,

nodes.name: GL(H)/U(H) corresponds to GL^+(H)
nodes.statement: If the unitary group $U(H)$ acts on $GL(H)$ by right multiplication, then the orbit space $\operatorname{GL}(H)/U(H)$ is in one-one correspondence with $GL^+(H)$.
nodes.statement_short: Modding out $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ by right unitary multiplication gives $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$.
assumptions: the unitary group $U(H)$ acts on $GL(H)$ by right multiplication
conclusions: the orbit space $\operatorname{GL}(H)/U(H)$ is in one-one correspondence with $GL^+(H)$.

nodes.name: Proof via the projection rho
nodes.statement: Since every positive operator $B\in\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ can be written in the form $B=AA^*$ with $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$, then $\rho$ is surjective. Let $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$ and $U\in U(H)$. We have \[ \rho(AU) = (AU)(AU)^* = AUU^*A^* = AIA^* = AA^* = \rho(A). \] In particular, we have \begin{align*} \ker(\rho) &= \{A\in\operatorname{GL}(H): \rho(A)=I\} \\ &= \{A\in\operatorname{GL}(H): AA^*=I\} \\ &= U(H). \end{align*} Since $\operatorname{GL}(H)/\ker(\rho)$ is in one-one correspondence with $\rho(\operatorname{GL}(H))=\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$, the quotient space follows.
nodes.statement_short: $\rho$ is surjective and right-$U(H)$-invariant with kernel $U(H)$, so the quotient by $\ker\rho$ is $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$.

nodes.name: Polar decomposition
nodes.statement: Therefore, $\operatorname{GL}(H) = \operatorname{GL}^+(H)U(H)$, which is to say that every operator in $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ can be factored into a positive operator in $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ and a unitary operator in $U(H)$. This is simply the polar decomposition of an operator.
nodes.statement_short: Every invertible operator factors as a positive invertible operator times a unitary.
conclusions: $\operatorname{GL}(H) = \operatorname{GL}^+(H)U(H)$

nodes.name: Banach space J = L^infty(X,H)
nodes.statement: We first define the Banach space $J$ to be \begin{equation} J = L^\infty(X, H) = \left\{f:X\mapsto H: \sup_{x\in X} \|f(x)\|_H <\infty\right\}, \end{equation} equipped with the norm \[ \|f\|_J = \sup_{x\in X} \|f(x)\|_H. \] where the subscripts indicate the space in which the norm is applied.
nodes.statement_short: $J$ is the space of bounded maps $X\to H$ with the sup norm.

nodes.name: Definition of J
nodes.statement: J = L^\infty(X, H) = \left\{f:X\mapsto H: \sup_{x\in X} \|f(x)\|_H <\infty\right\},

nodes.name: Spaces of frames F and Parseval frames F_0
nodes.statement: In addition, we define the spaces \begin{align} F &= \{f\in J: f \mbox{ is a frame}\} \\ F_0 &= \{f\in F: f \mbox{ is Parseval}\}. \end{align}

nodes.name: Definition of F and F_0
nodes.statement: F &= \{f\in J: f \mbox{ is a frame}\} \\ F_0 &= \{f\in F: f \mbox{ is Parseval}\}.

nodes.name: Existence of a Parseval frame
nodes.statement: Moreover, since $H$ is separable, it follows that $F_0$ is non-empty. That is, $H$ has at least one Parseval frame.
conclusions: $F_0$ is non-empty.

nodes.name: GL(H) acts boundedly on J
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$ and $f\in J$ and define the action of $A$ on $f$ by \[ (Af)(x) = A[f(x)]. \] Then $\operatorname{GL}(H)\subset \operatorname{GL}(J)$. That is, $A$ and $A^{-1}$ are bounded on $J$.
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise action of $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$ on $J$ is bounded with bounded inverse.
conclusions: Then $\operatorname{GL}(H)\subset \operatorname{GL}(J)$. That is, $A$ and $A^{-1}$ are bounded on $J$.

nodes.name: Proof by operator-norm bounds
nodes.statement:
We have the operator norm \[ \|A\|_J = \sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}  rac{\|Af\|_J}{\|f\|_J} = \sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}\sup_{x\in X}  rac{\|Af(x)\|_H}{\|f\|_J}. \] Since $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$, then we have  egin{align*} \sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}\sup_{x\in X}  rac{1}{\|A^{-1}\|_H} rac{\|f(x)\|_H}{\|f\|_J} \leq &\|A\|_J \leq \sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}\sup_{x\in X} \|A\|_H  rac{\|f(x)\|_H}{\|f\|_J} \  rac{1}{\|A^{-1}\|_H} \sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}\sup_{x\in X} rac{\|f(x)\|_H}{\|f\|_J} \leq &\|A\|_J \leq \|A\|_H\sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}\sup_{x\in X} rac{\|f(x)\|_H}{\|f\|_J} \  rac{1}{\|A^{-1}\|_H}\sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}  rac{\|f\|_J}{\|f\|_J} \leq &\|A\|_J \leq \|A\|_H\sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}  rac{\|f\|_J}{\|f\|_J} \  rac{1}{\|A^{-1}\|_H} \leq &\|A\|_J \leq \|A\|_H. \end{align*} Therefore, $A\in\operatorname{GL}(J)$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\|A\|_J$ between $1/\|A^{-1}\|_H$ and $\|A\|_H$ by taking suprema.

nodes.name: Frame operator map S
nodes.statement: Define the ``frame operator map'' $S:F\mapsto \operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ such that $S(f)$ is the frame operator of $f$.

nodes.name: Linear deformation of frames
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F$ and $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Then $Af\in F$ and the frame operator of $Af$ is $$S(Af) = \operatorname{ad}_A(S(f)) = AS(f)A^*.$$
nodes.statement_short: Applying $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$ to a frame gives a frame with frame operator $AS(f)A^*$.
conclusions: $Af\in F$
the frame operator of $Af$ is $$S(Af) = \operatorname{ad}_A(S(f)) = AS(f)A^*.$$
nodes.label: LinearDeform

nodes.name: Proof of linear deformation lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\phi\in H$. Then, $A^*\phi\in H$. Since $f$ is a frame, then \[ a\|A^*\phi\|_H^2 \leq \int_X\lvert\langle A^*\phi, f(x)\rangle_H\rvert^2\,d\mu(x) \leq b\|A^*\phi\|_H^2. \] Since $\langle A^*\phi,f(x)\rangle_H = \langle\phi, A[f(x)]\rangle_H = \langle\phi, (Af)(x)\rangle_H$, then \[ a\|A^*\phi\|_H^2 \leq \int_X\lvert\langle \phi, (Af)(x)\rangle_H\rvert^2\,d\mu(x) \leq b\|A^*\phi\|_H^2. \] Since $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$ and since $A$ and $A^*$ have the same norms, then we have \[ \frac{a}{\|A^{-1}\|_H^2}\|\phi\|_H^2 = a\left(\frac{\|\phi\|_H}{\|A^{-1}\|_H}\right)^2 \leq a\|A^*\phi\|_H^2. \] We also have \[ b\|A^*\phi\|_H^2 \leq b(\|A\|_H\|\phi\|_H)^2 = b\|A\|_H^2\|\phi\|_H^2. \] Therefore, for all $\phi\in H$, we have \[ \frac{a}{\|A^{-1}\|_H^2}\|\phi\|_H^2 \leq \int_X\lvert\phi,(Af)(x)\rangle_H^2\,d\mu(x) \leq b\|A\|_H^2\|\phi\|_H^2. \] Thus, $Af$ is a frame. The frame operator of $Af$ is given by \begin{align*} S(Af)\phi &= \int_X\langle\phi, (Af)(x)\rangle_H(Af)(x)\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \int_X\langle\phi,A[f(x)]\rangle_HA[f(x)]\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \int_X A\langle A^*\phi, f(x)\rangle_H f(x)\,d\mu(x). \end{align*} Since $A$ is bounded and hence uniformly continuous, then \begin{align*} S(Af)\phi &= A\int_X\langle A^*\phi, f(x)\rangle_H f(x)\,d\mu(x) \\ &= AS(f)A^*\phi. \end{align*} Therefore, $S(Af) = \operatorname{ad}_A(S)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the frame inequality to $A^*\phi$ and bound $\|A^*\phi\|$; then pull $A$ out of the frame-operator integral.

nodes.name: Fibration of frames into GL(H)-orbits
nodes.statement: The set of frames $F$ can therefore be fibrated into orbits under the action of $\operatorname{GL}(H)$.
conclusions: The set of frames $F$ can therefore be fibrated into orbits under the action of $\operatorname{GL}(H)$.

nodes.name: Orbit space F/GL(H)
nodes.statement: We let $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$ denote the resulting space of orbits.

nodes.name: Orbits are connected
nodes.statement: Note that since $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, the group $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ is topologically connected. As a consequence, the orbits in $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$ are connected spaces in $J$.

nodes.name: Orthonormal bases form exactly one orbit
nodes.statement: Because all orthonormal bases in $H$ are unitarily equivalent, exactly one orbit in $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$ is the space of all orthonormal bases in $H$. The elements of a frame in any other orbit are therefore necessarily linearly dependent.
assumptions: all orthonormal bases in $H$ are unitarily equivalent
conclusions: exactly one orbit in $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$ is the space of all orthonormal bases in $H$.
The elements of a frame in any other orbit are therefore necessarily linearly dependent.

nodes.name: Regularity of the GL(H) action
nodes.statement: Consider any $f\in F$ and $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Then $Af=f$ if and only if $A=I$. In other words, the action of $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ is regular on each orbit in $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$.
nodes.statement_short: $Af=f$ for a frame $f$ forces $A=I$: the action is free on each orbit.
conclusions: Then $Af=f$ if and only if $A=I$.
the action of $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ is regular on each orbit in $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$.
nodes.label: Regular

nodes.name: Proof by spanning of frame elements
nodes.statement: The reverse implication is trivial. For the forward implication, suppose $Af=f$. Recall $Af$ is defined by $(Af)(x) = A[f(x)]$ for all $x\in X$. Thus, $Af=f$ implies $A[f(x)] = f(x)$ for all $x\in X$. Since $f$ is a frame on $H$, the set $\{f(x):x\in X\}$ spans $H$. Since $A$ is linear on $H$, we have $A\phi = \phi$ for all $\phi\in H$.
nodes.statement_short: If $A$ fixes every $f(x)$ and the $f(x)$ span $H$, then $A=I$.

nodes.name: Orbits are principal homogeneous spaces
nodes.statement: Because the action of $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ is regular on each orbit in $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$, every orbit is a principal homogeneous space. Therefore, the linear transformation connecting two frames is unique.
assumptions: the action of $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ is regular on each orbit in $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$
conclusions: every orbit is a principal homogeneous space.
the linear transformation connecting two frames is unique.

nodes.name: Frame operator map is surjective
nodes.statement: The map $S$ is well-defined and surjective.
conclusions: The map $S$ is well-defined and surjective.

nodes.name: Proof by deforming a Parseval frame
nodes.statement: The frame operator $S(f)$ of a frame $f$ is positive, bounded, and has a bounded inverse. Hence, $S$ is well-defined. Let $B\in\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$. Then, $B=AA^*$ for some $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Let $f_0\in F_0$ be a Parseval frame, and define $f=Af_0$. By Lemma \ref{LinearDeform}, $f$ is a frame and \[ S(f) = S(Af_0) = \operatorname{ad}_A(S(f_0)) = \operatorname{ad}_A(I) = AA^* = B. \] Ergo, $S$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Write $B=AA^*$ and take $f=Af_0$ for a Parseval $f_0$; Lemma (linear deformation) gives $S(f)=B$.

nodes.name: Projection T onto Parseval frames
nodes.statement: Define the projection \begin{equation} T:F\mapsto F_0, \quad T(f) = S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of T
nodes.statement: T:F\mapsto F_0, \quad T(f) = S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f.

nodes.name: T is well-defined and surjective
nodes.statement: The map $T$ is well-defined and surjective.
conclusions: The map $T$ is well-defined and surjective.

nodes.name: Proof that T is a projection
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F$. By Lemma \ref{LinearDeform}, observe that \[ S(T(f)) = S(S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f) = S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}S(f) S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = I. \] Thus, $T(f)\in F_0$, and hence $T$ is well-defined. Note $T$ fixes $F_0$ pointwise: If $f\in F_0$, then $T(f)=I^{-\frac{1}{2}}f=f$. Thus, $T$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: By the deformation lemma $S(T(f))=I$, and $T$ fixes $F_0$ pointwise.

nodes.name: Parseval-preserving operators are unitary
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F_0$ and $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Then, $Af\in F_0$ if and only if $A\in U(H)$.
nodes.statement_short: An invertible operator maps a Parseval frame to a Parseval frame iff it is unitary.
conclusions: $Af\in F_0$ if and only if $A\in U(H)$.
nodes.label: UnitaryParseval

nodes.name: Proof via frame operator AA*
nodes.statement: First assume $Af\in F_0$. Then, \[ S(Af) = \operatorname{ad}_A(S(f)) = \operatorname{ad}_A(I) = AA^* = I. \] Hence, $A\in U(H)$. For the converse, suppose $A\in U(H)$. Then, $Af$ is a frame and \[ S(Af) = AA^* = I, \] so that $Af\in F_0$.

nodes.name: Parseval frames in an orbit are unitarily equivalent
nodes.statement: Therefore, all Parseval frames in a common orbit in $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$ are unitarily equivalent, and hence it is possible to linearly transform or ``project'' any frame to a Parseval frame that is unique up to unitary equivalence.
conclusions: all Parseval frames in a common orbit in $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$ are unitarily equivalent

nodes.name: Transversal of unitarily inequivalent Parseval frames
nodes.statement: Let $\overline{F}_0$ be a fixed transversal of the orbit space $F_0/U(H)$, so that $\overline{F}_0$ is a maximal set of unitarily inequivalent Parseval frames on $H$.

nodes.name: Unique factorization of Parseval frames
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{UnitaryParseval}, the ``factorization'' of a Parseval frame in $F_0$ into a unitary operator in $U(H)$ and a Parseval frame in $\overline{F}_0$ is unique.
conclusions: the ``factorization'' of a Parseval frame in $F_0$ into a unitary operator in $U(H)$ and a Parseval frame in $\overline{F}_0$ is unique.

nodes.name: Projection maps U and sigma
nodes.statement: We therefore define the projection maps \begin{equation} U:F_0\mapsto U(H) \mbox{ and } \sigma:F_0\mapsto \overline{F}_0 \mbox{ such that } f = U(f)\sigma(f) \mbox{ for all } f\in F_0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $U(f)$ and $\sigma(f)$ are the unitary and transversal factors in $f=U(f)\sigma(f)$.

nodes.name: Definition of U and sigma
nodes.statement: U:F_0\mapsto U(H) \mbox{ and } \sigma:F_0\mapsto \overline{F}_0 \mbox{ such that } f = U(f)\sigma(f) \mbox{ for all } f\in F_0.
nodes.label: Usigma

nodes.name: U and sigma are surjective
nodes.statement: We observe that for all $A\in U(H)$ and $f\in\overline{F}_0$, we have $U(Af)=A$ and $\sigma(Af)=f$. Thus, $U$ and $\sigma$ are both surjective.

nodes.name: Maps zeta and zeta^+
nodes.statement: First, we define the maps \begin{align} \zeta:\operatorname{GL}(H)\times\overline{F}_0\mapsto F, \quad &\zeta(A, f) = Af \\ \zeta^+:\operatorname{GL}^+(H)\times F_0\mapsto F, \quad &\zeta^+(A, f) = Af. \end{align}

nodes.name: Definition of zeta and zeta^+
nodes.statement: \zeta:\operatorname{GL}(H)\times\overline{F}_0\mapsto F, \quad &\zeta(A, f) = Af \\ \zeta^+:\operatorname{GL}^+(H)\times F_0\mapsto F, \quad &\zeta^+(A, f) = Af.

nodes.name: zeta and zeta^+ are continuous bijections
nodes.statement: The maps $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are continuous bijections.
conclusions: The maps $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are continuous bijections.
nodes.label: zeta

nodes.name: Proof that zeta, zeta^+ are continuous bijections
nodes.statement: First, we prove $\zeta$ is a bijection: Let $f\in F$. Since $T(f)\in F_0$, then $T(f)$ has the unique factorization $T(f) = U(T(f))\sigma(T(f))$. Note that $S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(T(f))\in \operatorname{GL}(H)$ and $\sigma(T(f))\in \overline{F}_0$. We have \begin{align*} \zeta(S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(T(f)), \sigma(T(f))) &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} U(T(f))\sigma(T(f)) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} T(f) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} f \\ &= f. \end{align*} Thus, $\zeta$ is surjective. Suppose $\zeta(A_1,f_1) = \zeta(A_2,f_2)$. Then, $A_1f_1=A_2f_2$, and hence $(A_2^{-1}A_1)f_1=f_2$. Since $f_1$ and $f_2$ are Parseval, then Lemma \ref{UnitaryParseval} implies that $A_2^{-1}A_1$ is unitary. But since $f_1,f_2\in\overline{F}_0$, then either $f_1$ and $f_2$ are unitarily inequivalent or $f_1=f_2$. Since $A_2^{-1}A_1\in U(H)$, then we must have $f_1=f_2$ and hence $A_2^{-1}A_1=I$ By Lemma \ref{Regular}. Thus, $A_1=A_2$. That is, $(A_1,f_1)=(A_2,f_2)$. Ergo, $\zeta$ is injective and therefore bijective. Now, we prove $\zeta^+$ is a bijection: Let $f\in F$. Note $S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}\in\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ and $T(f)\in F_0$. We have \begin{align*} \zeta^+(S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}, T(f)) &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} T(f) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} f \\ &= f. \end{align*} Thus, $\zeta^+$ is surjective. Suppose $\zeta^+(A_1,f_1)=\zeta^+(A_2,f_2)$. Thus, $A_1f_1=A_2f_2$, so that $(A_2^{-1}A_1)f_1=f_2$. Since $f_1$ and $f_2$ are Parseval, then Lemma \ref{UnitaryParseval} implies that $A_2^{-1}A_1$ is unitary. Thus, \[ (A_2^{-1}A_1)(A_2^{-1}A_1)^* = A_2^{-1}A_1A_1^*(A_2^{-1})^* = I. \] Since $A_2^{-1}$ and $A_1$ are positive and hence self-adjoint, then \begin{align*} A_2^{-1}A_1A_1A_2^{-1} &= I. \\ A_1^2 &= A_2^2. \end{align*} Since $A_1$ and $A_2$ are positive, then the unique principal square roots of $A_1^2$ and $A_2^2$ are precisely $A_1$ and $A_2$ respectively. Thus, we have $A_1=A_2$. This implies $A_2^{-1}A_1=I$, so that $f_1=f_2$. That is, $(A_1,f_1)=(A_2,f_2)$. Thus, $\zeta^+$ is injective and hence bijective. Finally, we prove $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are both continuous: Since $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are both restrictions of the map $\zeta_*:\operatorname{GL}(H)\times F_0\mapsto F$, then it suffices to show $\zeta_*$ is continuous. Let $\{(A_n,f_n)\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of points in $\operatorname{GL}(H)\times F_0$., and suppose $(A_n,f_n)\rightarrow (A,f)$. This means $A_n\rightarrow A$ and $f_n\rightarrow f$. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then, there exists $N_1\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N_1$ implies \[ \|A_n-A\|_H,\|f_n-f\|_J <\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}. \] Since $A_n\rightarrow A$, then there exists $N_2\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N_2$ implies $\|A_n\|_H<2\|A\|_H$. Assume $n>\max\{N_1,N_2\}$. Then, we have \begin{align*} \|\zeta_*(A_n,f_n)-\zeta_*(A,f)\|_J &= \|A_nf_n-Af\|_J \\ &= \|A_nf_n-A_nf+A_nf-Af\|_J \\ &\leq \|A_nf_n-A_nf\|_J+\|A_nf-Af\|_J \\ &= \sup_{x\in X} \|A_n(f_n-f)(x)\|_H+\sup_{x\in X} \|(A_n-A)f(x)\|_H \\ &\leq \|A_n\|_H \sup_{x\in X}\|(f_n-f)(x)\|_H + \|A_n-A\|_H\sup_{x\in X}\|f(x)\|_H \\ &= \|A_n\|_H\|f_n-f\|_J+\|A_n-A\|_H\|f\|_J \\ &< 2\|A\|_H\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}\right)+\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}\right)\|f\|_J \\ &= \varepsilon. \end{align*} Ergo, $\zeta_*$ and thus $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity by writing $f=S(f)^{1/2}T(f)$; injectivity via the unitary lemma, regularity and unique positive square roots; continuity by an $\varepsilon$ estimate. Key step: $f=S(f)^{1/2}U(T(f))\sigma(T(f))$.

nodes.name: Proof of the factorization corollary
nodes.statement: Because $\zeta:\operatorname{GL}(H)\times\overline{F}_0\mapsto F$ is a bijection, the orbit space $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$ is in one-one correspondence with $\overline{F}_0$. In other words, the transversal $\overline{F}_0$ of unitarily inequivalent Parseval frames indexes the orbits in $F$ induced by invertible linear transformations. In particular, because $\zeta$ is invertible, we have that $$F = \operatorname{GL}(H)\overline{F}_0,$$ with every frame having a unique representation in $\operatorname{GL}(H)\overline{F}_0$. Recalling the relationship between $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ and $\operatorname{GL}(H)$, the following corollary completes this line of thought.
nodes.statement_short: The bijection $\zeta$ gives $F=\operatorname{GL}(H)\overline F_0$ uniquely; combine with the polar decomposition.

nodes.name: Factorization of frames
nodes.statement: We have \[ F = \operatorname{GL}^+(H) U(H) \overline{F}_0 = \operatorname{GL}(H) \overline{F}_0 = \operatorname{GL}^+(H) F_0. \] Moreover, the factorization of a frame $f\in F$ in $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)U(H)\overline{F}_0$ as \[ f = S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(f)\sigma(T(f)) \] is unique.
nodes.statement_short: Every frame factors uniquely as positive operator, unitary, and transversal Parseval frame: $f=S(f)^{1/2}U(f)\sigma(T(f))$.
conclusions: \[ F = \operatorname{GL}^+(H) U(H) \overline{F}_0 = \operatorname{GL}(H) \overline{F}_0 = \operatorname{GL}^+(H) F_0. \]
the factorization of a frame $f\in F$ in $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)U(H)\overline{F}_0$ as \[ f = S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(f)\sigma(T(f)) \] is unique.
nodes.label: Factorization

nodes.name: Projections pi_1, pi_2
nodes.statement: Finally, we define the continuous projection maps \begin{align*} \pi_1:\operatorname{GL}(H)\times F_0\mapsto \operatorname{GL}(H), \quad &\pi_1(A, f) = A \\ \pi_2:\operatorname{GL}(H)\times F_0\mapsto F_0, \quad &\pi_2(A, f) = f. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Identity via zeta and projections
nodes.statement: For all $f\in F$, we have \[ f = \zeta(\pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f)), \pi_2(\zeta^{-1}(f))). \]
nodes.label: Identity

nodes.name: Fiber bundle
nodes.statement: Let $E_1$ and $B$ be topological spaces. A topological space $E$ is a called \emph{fiber bundle} with base space $B$ and fiber $E_1$ if there exists a \emph{projection} or continuous surjection $\pi:E\mapsto B$ that satisfies the \emph{local triviality condition}: For every $x\in E$, there is an open neighborhood $U\subseteq B$ about $\pi(x)$ and a homeomorphism $\theta:\pi^{-1}(U)\mapsto U\times E_1$ such that \[ \pi(x) = (\pi_U\circ\theta)(x), \quad\forall x\in \pi^{-1}(U), \] where $\pi_U:U\times E_1\mapsto U$ is the natural projection from the product space $U\times E_1$ to the first factor $B$. If the fiber $E_1$ is a principal homogeneous space under the action of a group $G$, then $E$ is called a \emph{principal fiber bundle} with \emph{structure group} $G$.
differentia: there exists a \emph{projection} or continuous surjection $\pi:E\mapsto B$ that satisfies the \emph{local triviality condition}
nodes.statement_short: A space with a continuous surjection to $B$ that is locally a product $U\times E_1$; principal when the fiber is a principal homogeneous $G$-space.

nodes.name: Product spaces and the Mobius strip
nodes.statement: Every product space $E = B\times E_1$ is a fiber bundle with base space either $B$ or $E_1$. A less trivial example of a fiber bundle is the M\"{o}bius strip with base space the circle $S^1$ and fiber $[0, 1]$.

nodes.name: Fiber F_1
nodes.statement: Proceeding, we fix some Parseval frame $f_{10}\in\overline{F}_0$ and define the space \begin{equation} F_1 = \operatorname{GL}(H)f_{10} = \{Af_{10}: A\in \operatorname{GL}(H)\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $F_1$ is the $\operatorname{GL}(H)$-orbit of a fixed Parseval frame $f_{10}\in\overline F_0$.

nodes.name: Definition of F_1
nodes.statement: F_1 = \operatorname{GL}(H)f_{10} = \{Af_{10}: A\in \operatorname{GL}(H)\}.
nodes.label: F1

nodes.name: Projection T_1
nodes.statement: Consequently, we define the projection map \begin{equation} T_1:F\mapsto F_1, \quad T_1(f) = \pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f))f_{10}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of T_1
nodes.statement: T_1:F\mapsto F_1, \quad T_1(f) = \pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f))f_{10}.
nodes.label: T1

nodes.name: T_1 is surjective
nodes.statement: The map $T_1$ is surjective.
conclusions: The map $T_1$ is surjective.
nodes.label: T1Surjection

nodes.name: Proof of surjectivity of T_1
nodes.statement: Let $f_1\in F_1$. By Corollary \ref{Identity}, we have \begin{align*} f_1 &= \zeta(\pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f_1)), \pi_2(\zeta^{-1}(f_1))) \\ &= \zeta(\pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f_1)), f_{10}) \\ &= \pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f_1)) f_{10} \\ &= T_1(f_1). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the identity corollary to $f_1\in F_1$: $T_1(f_1)=f_1$.

nodes.name: F_1 corresponds to GL(H)
nodes.statement: Since $F_1$ is a principal homogeneous space under the action of $\operatorname{GL}(H)$, it follows that $F_1$ and $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ are in one-one correspondence.
assumptions: $F_1$ is a principal homogeneous space under the action of $\operatorname{GL}(H)$
conclusions: $F_1$ and $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ are in one-one correspondence.

nodes.name: Map theta
nodes.statement: Next, we define the map \begin{equation} \theta:F_1\mapsto\operatorname{GL}(H), \quad \theta(f) = \pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f)). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of theta
nodes.statement: \theta:F_1\mapsto\operatorname{GL}(H), \quad \theta(f) = \pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f)).

nodes.name: theta is a bijection
nodes.statement: The map $\theta$ is a bijection.
conclusions: The map $\theta$ is a bijection.
nodes.label: theta

nodes.name: Proof that theta is a bijection
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Then, $Af_{10}\in F_1$. By Corollary \ref{Identity}, we have \begin{align*} Af_{10} &= \zeta(\pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(Af_{10})), \pi_2(\zeta^{-1}(Af_{10}))) \\ &= \zeta(\theta(Af_{10})), f_{10}) \\ &= \theta(Af_{10})f_{10}. \end{align*} But since $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ acts regularly on $F_1$ (by Lemma \ref{Regular}), then $\theta(Af_{10})=A$. Ergo, $\theta$ is surjective. Suppose $\theta(f_1) = \theta(f_2)$. As above, $f_1$ and $f_2$ have the unique factorizations $f_1=\theta(f_1)f_{10}$ and $f_2=\theta(f_2)f_{10}$. But since $\theta(f_1)=\theta(f_2)$, then \[ f_1 = \theta(f_1)f_{10} = \theta(f_2)f_{10} = f_2. \] Thus, $\theta$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity via the identity corollary and regularity of the action; injectivity from $f=\theta(f)f_{10}$.

nodes.name: Lifted map theta_*
nodes.statement: The bijection $\theta$ may be lifted to the map \begin{equation} \theta_*:F_1\times\overline{F}_0\mapsto F, \quad \theta_*(f_1, f_0) = \zeta(\theta(f_1), f_0). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of theta_*
nodes.statement: \theta_*:F_1\times\overline{F}_0\mapsto F, \quad \theta_*(f_1, f_0) = \zeta(\theta(f_1), f_0).

nodes.name: theta_* is a bijection with explicit inverse
nodes.statement: The map $\theta_*$ is a bijection and has inverse \[ \theta^{-1}(f) = (T_1(f), \sigma\circ T(f)). \]
nodes.statement_short: $\theta_*:F_1\times\overline F_0\to F$ is bijective with inverse $(T_1,\sigma\circ T)$.
conclusions: The map $\theta_*$ is a bijection
has inverse \[ \theta^{-1}(f) = (T_1(f), \sigma\circ T(f)). \]

nodes.name: Proof via theta and zeta bijections
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{theta}, $\theta$ is bijective. The identity map is obviously bijective. Thus, the map \[ (f_1,f_0)\rightarrow (\theta(f_1), f_0) \] is a bijection from $F_1\times\overline{F}_0$ to $\operatorname{GL}(H)\times\overline{F}_0$. By Theorem \ref{zeta}, $\zeta$ is bijective. Ergo, $\theta_*$ is a bijection. To verify that the expression $\theta_*^{-1}$ is indeed the inverse of $\theta_*$, let $f\in F$ and consider \begin{align*} \theta_*(\theta_*^{-1}(f)) &= \zeta(\theta(T_1(f)), \sigma\circ T(f)) \\ &= \zeta[\pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}(\pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}(f)f_{10}), \sigma\circ T(f)] \\ &= \zeta(\pi_1\zeta^{-1}(f), \sigma\circ T(f)) \\ &= \pi_1(\zeta(f))\sigma(T(f)) \\ &= f. \end{align*} The reverse composition proceeds similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Compose the bijection $\theta\times\mathrm{id}$ with $\zeta$; verify the inverse by direct computation.

nodes.name: Continuity of zeta^{-1} gives a principal fiber bundle
nodes.statement: If $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous, then $\theta_*:F_1\times\overline{F}_0\mapsto F$ is a homeomorphism and $F$ is a principal fiber bundle with base space $\overline{F}_0$, fiber $F_1$, and structure group $\operatorname{GL}(H)$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous, $F\cong F_1\times\overline F_0$ is a principal $\operatorname{GL}(H)$-bundle over $\overline F_0$.
conclusions: $\theta_*:F_1\times\overline{F}_0\mapsto F$ is a homeomorphism
$F$ is a principal fiber bundle with base space $\overline{F}_0$, fiber $F_1$, and structure group $\operatorname{GL}(H)$.
nodes.label: IfzetaCont

nodes.name: Proof by continuity of components
nodes.statement: Suppose $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous. Then, $\theta = \pi_1\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous. By Theorem \ref{zeta}, $\zeta$ is continuous. Thus, $\theta_*(f_1,f_0) = \zeta(\theta(f_1), f_0)$ is continuous Since $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous, then $T_1(f) = \pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f))f_{10}$ and $\sigma\circ T = \pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}$ are continuous. Thus, $\theta_*^{-1} = (T_1, \sigma\circ T)$ is continuous. Ergo, $\theta_*$ is a homeomorphism. Since $F$ is homeomorphic to the product space $F_1\times\overline{F}_0$ (via $\theta_*^{-1}$), then $F$ is trivially a fiber bundle as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of $\zeta^{-1}$ makes $\theta_*$ and its inverse continuous, so $F$ is homeomorphic to a product.

nodes.name: Banach space J_1 = L^1(X,H)
nodes.statement: We first define the Banach space \[ J_1 = L^1(X, H) \] equipped with the norm \[ \|f\|_{J_1} = \int_X \|f(x)\|_H\,d\mu(x). \]

nodes.name: All frames are integrable
nodes.statement: Suppose that $F\subset J_1$. That is, suppose that all frames (in $J$) on $H$ are integrable.

nodes.name: Formula for zeta^{-1}
nodes.statement: By the commuting diagram in Section 2 and the unique factorization granted by Corollary \ref{Factorization}, it is straightforward to show that $\zeta^{-1}:F\mapsto\operatorname{GL}(H)\times\overline{F}_0$ is given by \begin{equation} \zeta^{-1}(f) = (S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(f), \sigma\circ T(f)). \end{equation}
conclusions: $\zeta^{-1}:F\mapsto\operatorname{GL}(H)\times\overline{F}_0$ is given by

nodes.name: Formula for zeta inverse
nodes.statement: \zeta^{-1}(f) = (S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(f), \sigma\circ T(f)).

nodes.name: Continuity of the frame operator map in J_1
nodes.statement: The map $S:F\mapsto\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$.
conclusions: The map $S:F\mapsto\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$.
nodes.label: SCont

nodes.name: Epsilon estimate for S
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of frames in $F$ and $f\in F$ such that $f_n\rightarrow f$ in $J_1$. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then, there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N$ implies $\|f_n\|_{J_1}<2\|f\|_{j_1}$ and \[ \|f_n-f\|_{J_1} < \frac{\varepsilon}{3\|f\|_{J_1}}. \] Suppose $n>N$. Consider any $\phi\in H$. We have \begin{align*} \|S(f_n)\phi-S(f)\phi\|_H &= \left\|\int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f_n(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ &= \left\|\int_X \brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f_n(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right. \\ & \qquad + \left.\int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ &= \left\|\int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H [f_n(x)-f(x)]\,d\mu(x) + \int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)-f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ & \leq \int_X \|\phi\|_H\|f_n(x)\|_H\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H\,d\mu(x) \\ & \qquad + \int_X\|\phi\|_H\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H\|f\|_H\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \|\phi\|\int_X \|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H (\|f_n(x)\|_H+\|f(x)\|_H)\,d\mu(x). \end{align*} By H\"{o}lder's Inequality, we have \begin{align*} \|S(f_n)\phi-S(f)\phi\|_H &\leq \|\phi\|_H\int_X\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H\,d\mu(x)\int_X(\|f_n(x)\|_H+\|f(x)\|_H)\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \|\phi\|_H\|f_n-f\|_{J_1}(\|f_n\|_{J_1}+\|f\|_{J_1}) \\ &< 3\|f\|_{J_1}\|f_n-f\|_{J_1}\|\phi\|_H \\ &< \varepsilon \|\phi\|_H. \end{align*} Since this holds for all $\phi\in H$, then $\|S(f_n)-S(f)\|_H<\varepsilon$. Ergo, $S(f_n)\rightarrow S(f)$, and hence $S$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Split $S(f_n)-S(f)$ by adding and subtracting a cross term and bound the integrals in $J_1$ norms.

nodes.name: Continuity of T in J_1
nodes.statement: The map $T:F\mapsto F_0$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$.
conclusions: The map $T:F\mapsto F_0$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$.
nodes.label: TCont

nodes.name: Epsilon estimate for T
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of frames in $F$ and $f\in F$ such that $f_n\rightarrow f$ in $J_1$. By Lemma \ref{SCont}, $S(f_n)\rightarrow S(f)$. Since the map sending an operator in $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ to its inverse and the map sending an operator in $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ to its principal square root are both continuous in the operator norm, then $S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\rightarrow S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then, there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N$ implies $\|f_n\|_{J_1}<2\|f\|_{J_1}$ and \[ \|f-f_n\|_{J_1},\|S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H < \delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|f\|_{J_1}+\|S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H}. \] Suppose $n>N$. We have \begin{align*} \|T(f_n)-T(f)\|_{J_1} &= \|S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f_n-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f\|_{J_1} \\ &= \|S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f_n-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f_n+S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f_n-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f\|_{J_1} \\ &= \|[S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}]f_n+S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(f_n-f)\|_{J_1} \\ &\leq \|S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H\|f_n\|_{J_1}+\|S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H\|f_n-f\|_{J_1} \\ &< \delta 2\|f\|_{J_1} + \|S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H\delta \\ &= \varepsilon. \end{align*} Ergo, $T(f_n)\rightarrow T(f)$, and hence $T$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of $S$, inversion and square root gives $S(f_n)^{-1/2}\to S(f)^{-1/2}$; then a triangle-inequality estimate.

nodes.name: Continuous transversal
nodes.statement: Suppose $\overline{F}_0$ is a continuous transversal of $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$. That is, suppose that the projection $\sigma:F_0\mapsto\overline{F}_0$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$.

nodes.name: Continuity of U in J_1
nodes.statement: The map $U:F_0\mapsto U(H)$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$.
conclusions: The map $U:F_0\mapsto U(H)$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$.
nodes.label: UCont

nodes.name: Proof via U(f) = V_f^* V_sigma(f)
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F_0$. Then, $f_0$ has the unique factorization $f = U(f)\sigma(f)$. For any $\phi\in H$ and for all $x\in X$, we have \[ \brak{\phi, f(x)}_H = \brak{\phi, U(f)\sigma(f)(x)}_H = \brak{U(f)^*\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H. \] Letting $V_g$ and $V_g^*$ denote the analysis and synthesis operators of a frame $g\in F$, we have \[ V_f\phi = V_{\sigma(f)}U(f)^*\phi, \] or simply $V_f = V_{\sigma(f)}U(f)^*$. Thus, $V_fU(f) = V_{\sigma(f)}$, and hence $V_f^*V_fU(f) = V_f^*V_{\sigma(f)}$. But since $f$ is Parseval, then $V_f^*V_f = S(f)=I$ so that \[ U(f) = V_f^* V_{\sigma(f)}. \] Thus, for all $\phi\in H$, we have \begin{equation} U(f)\phi = \int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x). \end{equation} To show $U$ is continuous, let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of frames in $F_0$ and $f\in F_0$ with $f_n\rightarrow f$ in $J_1$. Since $\sigma$ is continuous, then $\sigma(f_n)\rightarrow\sigma(f)$. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then, there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N$ implies $\|f_n\|_{J_1}<2\|f\|_{J_1}$ and \[ \|f_n-f\|_{J_1}, \|\sigma(f_n)-\sigma(f)\|_{J_1} < \delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{\|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1}+2\|f\|_{J_1}}. \] Suppose $n>N$. Let $\phi\in H$. By manipulations similar to those used in the proof of Lemma \ref{SCont} (including the Triangle Inequality, Cauchy-Schwartz Inequality, and H\"{o}lder's Inequality), we have \begin{align*} \|U(f_n)\phi-U(f)\phi\|_H &= \left\|\int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f_n)(x)}_H f_n(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ &\leq \|\phi\|_H \|\sigma(f_n)-\sigma(f)\|_{J_1}\|f_n\|_{J_1} + \|\phi\|_H \|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1} \|f_n-f\|_{J_1} \\ &< \|\phi\|_H \delta 2\|f\|_{J_1} + \|\phi\|_H \|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1} \delta \\ &= (2\|f\|_{J_1}+\|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1})\delta \|\phi\|_H \\ &= \varepsilon \|\phi\|_H. \end{align*} Since this holds for all $\phi\in H$, then $\|U(f_n)-U(f)\|_H < \varepsilon$. Ergo, $U(f_n)\rightarrow U(f)$, and hence $U$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Express $U(f)=V_f^*V_{\sigma(f)}$ as an integral, then estimate as for $S$ using continuity of $\sigma$.

nodes.name: Integral formula for U(f)
nodes.statement: U(f)\phi = \int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x).

nodes.name: Frames form a principal fiber bundle
nodes.statement: The map $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$. Moreover, $F$ is a principal fiber bundle with base space $\overline{F}_0$, fiber $F_1$, and structure group $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ in the topology of $J_1$.
nodes.statement_short: In the $J_1$ topology $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous and $F$ is a principal $\operatorname{GL}(H)$-bundle over $\overline F_0$ with fiber $F_1$.
conclusions: The map $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$.
$F$ is a principal fiber bundle with base space $\overline{F}_0$, fiber $F_1$, and structure group $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ in the topology of $J_1$.
nodes.label: FiberBundle

nodes.name: Proof by continuity of S, T, U
nodes.statement: Recall that $\zeta^{-1}$ is given by \[ \zeta^{-1}(f) = (S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(f), \sigma\circ T(f)). \] By Lemmas \ref{SCont}-\ref{UCont}, the maps $S$, $T$, and $U$ are continuous in $J_1$. Moreover, $\sigma$ and the square root function are continuous as well. Therefore, $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous. By Proposition \ref{IfzetaCont}, $F$ is a fiber bundle as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: $\zeta^{-1}=(S^{1/2}U,\sigma\circ T)$ is continuous by the three continuity lemmas; conclude with the bundle criterion.

nodes.name: Proof of the finite-measure corollary
nodes.statement: A special case occurs when $\mu$ is a finite measure on $X$. In this case, convergence in $J=L^\infty(X,H)$ implies convergence in $J_1=L^1(X,H)$. We therefore have the following corollary.
nodes.statement_short: For finite $\mu$, $L^\infty$ convergence implies $L^1$ convergence, so the $J_1$ result transfers.

nodes.name: Fiber bundle for finite measures
nodes.statement: If $\mu$ is a finite measure on $X$, then the space $F$ is a principal fiber bundle in the topologies of both $J$ and $J_1$.
conclusions: the space $F$ is a principal fiber bundle in the topologies of both $J$ and $J_1$.
nodes.label: FiniteMeasure

nodes.name: Finite frames form a principal fiber bundle
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be finite-dimensional and $X$ be a finite set with counting measure $\mu$. Then the space $F$ of all finite frames on $H$ indexed by $X$ is a principal fiber bundle with base space $\overline{F}_0$, fiber $F_1$, and structure group $\operatorname{GL}(H)$.
assumptions: Let $H$ be finite-dimensional and $X$ be a finite set with counting measure $\mu$.
conclusions: the space $F$ of all finite frames on $H$ indexed by $X$ is a principal fiber bundle with base space $\overline{F}_0$, fiber $F_1$, and structure group $\operatorname{GL}(H)$.

nodes.name: Frame matrix
nodes.statement: For example, if $X=\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\} $ where $n\geq m>0,$ then we will say that an $n\times m$ matrix $T$ is a \emph{frame matrix}, or simply a \emph{frame} if the context is understood, if the set of columns obtained by Hermitian transposing its rows are a frame.
differentia: the set of columns obtained by Hermitian transposing its rows are a frame

nodes.name: SVD of a frame matrix
nodes.statement: A frame matrix has a singular value decomposition of \[ T=U\tilde{\Sigma}V^{\ast }\ \ where\ \ \tilde{\Sigma}= \left[ \begin{array}{c} \Sigma \\ 0 \end{array} \right] \] Moreover, $\tilde{\Sigma}$ is itself a frame, and if $\Sigma =I_{m},$ then $\tilde{\Sigma}$ is also a Parseval frame.
conclusions: $\tilde{\Sigma}$ is itself a frame
$\tilde{\Sigma}$ is also a Parseval frame.

nodes.name: Base space from matrices with one non-zero entry per row
nodes.statement: Instead, if we define $M_{\Sigma }$ to be the set of $n\times m$ matrices whose rows have at most a single non-zero entry and whose columns are unit vectors in $\mathbb{C}^{n}$, then a choice of base space $\bar{F}_{0}$ for $X=\left\{1,\ldots n\right\} $ over $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ is a maximally non-unitary subset of $M_{\Sigma }$ (there are matrices in $M_{\Sigma }$ that are unitarily equivalent).
nodes.statement_short: With $M_\Sigma$ the $n\times m$ matrices with at most one non-zero per row and unit columns, a base space $\overline F_0$ is a maximal unitarily inequivalent subset of $M_\Sigma$.
assumptions: we define $M_{\Sigma }$ to be the set of $n\times m$ matrices whose rows have at most a single non-zero entry and whose columns are unit vectors in $\mathbb{C}^{n}$
conclusions: a choice of base space $\bar{F}_{0}$ for $X=\left\{1,\ldots n\right\} $ over $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ is a maximally non-unitary subset of $M_{\Sigma }$

nodes.name: Form of finite Parseval frames and frames
nodes.statement: It follows that every Parseval frame over $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ with $n$ elements is of the form \[ F=TV^{\ast },\ \ \ T\in M_{\Sigma } \] and similarly, every frame with $n$ elements is of the form $TG,$ where $T\in M_{\Sigma }$ and $G\in GL\left( \mathbb{C}^{m}\right) .$
nodes.statement_short: Every $n$-element Parseval frame on $\mathbb{C}^m$ is $TV^*$ and every frame is $TG$ with $T\in M_\Sigma$, $G$ invertible.
conclusions: every Parseval frame over $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ with $n$ elements is of the form \[ F=TV^{\ast },\ \ \ T\in M_{\Sigma } \]
every frame with $n$ elements is of the form $TG,$ where $T\in M_{\Sigma }$ and $G\in GL\left( \mathbb{C}^{m}\right) .$

nodes.name: Reflexivity and symmetry
nodes.statement: Let $B\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Clearly, $\operatorname{ad}_I(B)=IBI^*=B$, so that $B\sim B$. Thus, $\sim$ is reflexive. Given $B,B^\prime\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$, suppose $B\sim B^\prime$. That is, $ad_A(B)=ABA*=B^\prime$ for some $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Then, \[ \operatorname{ad}_{A^{-1}}(B^\prime) = A^{-1}B^\prime (A^{-1})^* = A^{-1}ABA^*(A^*)^{-1} = B. \] Thus, $B^\prime\sim B$, and hence $\sim$ is symmetric.

nodes.name: Transitivity
nodes.statement: Finally, suppose $B\sim B^\prime$ and $B^\prime\sim B^{\prime\prime}$. Thus, $\operatorname{ad}_A(B)=ABA^*=B^\prime$ and $\operatorname{ad}_{A^\prime}(B^\prime)=A^\prime B^\prime (A^\prime)^*=B^{\prime\prime}$ for some $A,A^\prime\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Then, \[ \operatorname{ad}_{A^\prime A}(B) = A^\prime AB(A^\prime A)^* = A^\prime (ABA^*)(A^\prime)^* = A^\prime B^\prime (A^\prime)^* = B^{\prime\prime}. \] Thus, $B\sim B^{\prime\prime}$, and hence $\sim$ is transitive.

nodes.name: Closure under adjugation
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$ and $B\in\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$. For any $\phi\in H$, we have \[ \brak{\operatorname{ad}_A(B)\phi, \phi} = \brak{ABA^*\phi, \phi} = \brak{BA^*\phi, A^*\phi}\geq 0, \] where the inequality holds since $A^*\phi\in H$ and $B$ is positive. Thus, $\operatorname{ad}_A(B)$ is positive, so that $GL^+(H)$ is closed under adjugation.

nodes.name: Any two positives are adjugate
nodes.statement: Let $B,C\in\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$. Since $B,C$ are positive, then $B=SS^*$ and $C=TT^*$ for some $S,T\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. There exists $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$ such that $T=AS$. We have \[ \operatorname{ad}_A(B) = ABA^* = ASS^*A^* = (AS)(AS)^* = TT^* = C. \] Thus, $B\sim C$.
nodes.statement_short: Relate two positive operators by $\operatorname{ad}_A$ with $T=AS$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Ergo, $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ is an adjugacy class.

nodes.name: Surjectivity of rho
nodes.statement: Since every positive operator $B\in\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ can be written in the form $B=AA^*$ with $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$, then $\rho$ is surjective.

nodes.name: Kernel of rho
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$ and $U\in U(H)$. We have \[ \rho(AU) = (AU)(AU)^* = AUU^*A^* = AIA^* = AA^* = \rho(A). \] In particular, we have \begin{align*} \ker(\rho) &= \{A\in\operatorname{GL}(H): \rho(A)=I\} \\ &= \{A\in\operatorname{GL}(H): AA^*=I\} \\ &= U(H). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Since $\operatorname{GL}(H)/\ker(\rho)$ is in one-one correspondence with $\rho(\operatorname{GL}(H))=\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$, the quotient space follows.

nodes.name: Operator norm
nodes.statement: We have the operator norm \[ \|A\|_J = \sup_{f\in J,f\neq 0} \frac{\|Af\|_J}{\|f\|_J} = \sup_{f\in J,f\neq 0}\sup_{x\in X} \frac{\|Af(x)\|_H}{\|f\|_J}. \]

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Therefore, $A\in\operatorname{GL}(J)$.

nodes.name: Af is a frame
nodes.statement: Let $\phi\in H$. Then, $A^*\phi\in H$. Since $f$ is a frame, then \[ a\|A^*\phi\|_H^2 \leq \int_X\lvert\langle A^*\phi, f(x)\rangle_H\rvert^2\,d\mu(x) \leq b\|A^*\phi\|_H^2. \] Since $\langle A^*\phi,f(x)\rangle_H = \langle\phi, A[f(x)]\rangle_H = \langle\phi, (Af)(x)\rangle_H$, then \[ a\|A^*\phi\|_H^2 \leq \int_X\lvert\langle \phi, (Af)(x)\rangle_H\rvert^2\,d\mu(x) \leq b\|A^*\phi\|_H^2. \] Since $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$ and since $A$ and $A^*$ have the same norms, then we have \[ \frac{a}{\|A^{-1}\|_H^2}\|\phi\|_H^2 = a\left(\frac{\|\phi\|_H}{\|A^{-1}\|_H}\right)^2 \leq a\|A^*\phi\|_H^2. \] We also have \[ b\|A^*\phi\|_H^2 \leq b(\|A\|_H\|\phi\|_H)^2 = b\|A\|_H^2\|\phi\|_H^2. \] Therefore, for all $\phi\in H$, we have \[ \frac{a}{\|A^{-1}\|_H^2}\|\phi\|_H^2 \leq \int_X\lvert\phi,(Af)(x)\rangle_H^2\,d\mu(x) \leq b\|A\|_H^2\|\phi\|_H^2. \] Thus, $Af$ is a frame.

nodes.name: Frame operator of Af
nodes.statement: The frame operator of $Af$ is given by \begin{align*} S(Af)\phi &= \int_X\langle\phi, (Af)(x)\rangle_H(Af)(x)\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \int_X\langle\phi,A[f(x)]\rangle_HA[f(x)]\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \int_X A\langle A^*\phi, f(x)\rangle_H f(x)\,d\mu(x). \end{align*} Since $A$ is bounded and hence uniformly continuous, then \begin{align*} S(Af)\phi &= A\int_X\langle A^*\phi, f(x)\rangle_H f(x)\,d\mu(x) \\ &= AS(f)A^*\phi. \end{align*} Therefore, $S(Af) = \operatorname{ad}_A(S)$.

nodes.name: Pointwise fixing
nodes.statement: The reverse implication is trivial. For the forward implication, suppose $Af=f$. Recall $Af$ is defined by $(Af)(x) = A[f(x)]$ for all $x\in X$. Thus, $Af=f$ implies $A[f(x)] = f(x)$ for all $x\in X$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Since $f$ is a frame on $H$, the set $\{f(x):x\in X\}$ spans $H$. Since $A$ is linear on $H$, we have $A\phi = \phi$ for all $\phi\in H$.

nodes.name: Well-defined
nodes.statement: The frame operator $S(f)$ of a frame $f$ is positive, bounded, and has a bounded inverse. Hence, $S$ is well-defined.

nodes.name: Construction
nodes.statement: Let $B\in\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$. Then, $B=AA^*$ for some $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Let $f_0\in F_0$ be a Parseval frame, and define $f=Af_0$.

nodes.name: Surjectivity
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{LinearDeform}, $f$ is a frame and \[ S(f) = S(Af_0) = \operatorname{ad}_A(S(f_0)) = \operatorname{ad}_A(I) = AA^* = B. \] Ergo, $S$ is surjective.

nodes.name: Well-defined
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F$. By Lemma \ref{LinearDeform}, observe that \[ S(T(f)) = S(S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f) = S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}S(f) S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = I. \] Thus, $T(f)\in F_0$, and hence $T$ is well-defined.

nodes.name: Surjective
nodes.statement: Note $T$ fixes $F_0$ pointwise: If $f\in F_0$, then $T(f)=I^{-\frac{1}{2}}f=f$. Thus, $T$ is surjective.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: First assume $Af\in F_0$. Then, \[ S(Af) = \operatorname{ad}_A(S(f)) = \operatorname{ad}_A(I) = AA^* = I. \] Hence, $A\in U(H)$.

nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement: For the converse, suppose $A\in U(H)$. Then, $Af$ is a frame and \[ S(Af) = AA^* = I, \] so that $Af\in F_0$.

nodes.name: zeta bijective
nodes.statement: First, we prove $\zeta$ is a bijection: Let $f\in F$. Since $T(f)\in F_0$, then $T(f)$ has the unique factorization $T(f) = U(T(f))\sigma(T(f))$. Note that $S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(T(f))\in \operatorname{GL}(H)$ and $\sigma(T(f))\in \overline{F}_0$. We have \begin{align*} \zeta(S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(T(f)), \sigma(T(f))) &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} U(T(f))\sigma(T(f)) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} T(f) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} f \\ &= f. \end{align*} Thus, $\zeta$ is surjective. Suppose $\zeta(A_1,f_1) = \zeta(A_2,f_2)$. Then, $A_1f_1=A_2f_2$, and hence $(A_2^{-1}A_1)f_1=f_2$. Since $f_1$ and $f_2$ are Parseval, then Lemma \ref{UnitaryParseval} implies that $A_2^{-1}A_1$ is unitary. But since $f_1,f_2\in\overline{F}_0$, then either $f_1$ and $f_2$ are unitarily inequivalent or $f_1=f_2$. Since $A_2^{-1}A_1\in U(H)$, then we must have $f_1=f_2$ and hence $A_2^{-1}A_1=I$ By Lemma \ref{Regular}. Thus, $A_1=A_2$. That is, $(A_1,f_1)=(A_2,f_2)$. Ergo, $\zeta$ is injective and therefore bijective.

nodes.name: zeta surjective
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F$. Since $T(f)\in F_0$, then $T(f)$ has the unique factorization $T(f) = U(T(f))\sigma(T(f))$. Note that $S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(T(f))\in \operatorname{GL}(H)$ and $\sigma(T(f))\in \overline{F}_0$. We have \begin{align*} \zeta(S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(T(f)), \sigma(T(f))) &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} U(T(f))\sigma(T(f)) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} T(f) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} f \\ &= f. \end{align*} Thus, $\zeta$ is surjective.

nodes.name: zeta injective
nodes.statement: Suppose $\zeta(A_1,f_1) = \zeta(A_2,f_2)$. Then, $A_1f_1=A_2f_2$, and hence $(A_2^{-1}A_1)f_1=f_2$. Since $f_1$ and $f_2$ are Parseval, then Lemma \ref{UnitaryParseval} implies that $A_2^{-1}A_1$ is unitary. But since $f_1,f_2\in\overline{F}_0$, then either $f_1$ and $f_2$ are unitarily inequivalent or $f_1=f_2$. Since $A_2^{-1}A_1\in U(H)$, then we must have $f_1=f_2$ and hence $A_2^{-1}A_1=I$ By Lemma \ref{Regular}. Thus, $A_1=A_2$. That is, $(A_1,f_1)=(A_2,f_2)$. Ergo, $\zeta$ is injective and therefore bijective.
nodes.statement_short: Unitary lemma and regularity give injectivity

nodes.name: zeta+ bijective
nodes.statement: Now, we prove $\zeta^+$ is a bijection: Let $f\in F$. Note $S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}\in\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ and $T(f)\in F_0$. We have \begin{align*} \zeta^+(S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}, T(f)) &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} T(f) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} f \\ &= f. \end{align*} Thus, $\zeta^+$ is surjective. Suppose $\zeta^+(A_1,f_1)=\zeta^+(A_2,f_2)$. Thus, $A_1f_1=A_2f_2$, so that $(A_2^{-1}A_1)f_1=f_2$. Since $f_1$ and $f_2$ are Parseval, then Lemma \ref{UnitaryParseval} implies that $A_2^{-1}A_1$ is unitary. Thus, \[ (A_2^{-1}A_1)(A_2^{-1}A_1)^* = A_2^{-1}A_1A_1^*(A_2^{-1})^* = I. \] Since $A_2^{-1}$ and $A_1$ are positive and hence self-adjoint, then \begin{align*} A_2^{-1}A_1A_1A_2^{-1} &= I. \\ A_1^2 &= A_2^2. \end{align*} Since $A_1$ and $A_2$ are positive, then the unique principal square roots of $A_1^2$ and $A_2^2$ are precisely $A_1$ and $A_2$ respectively. Thus, we have $A_1=A_2$. This implies $A_2^{-1}A_1=I$, so that $f_1=f_2$. That is, $(A_1,f_1)=(A_2,f_2)$. Thus, $\zeta^+$ is injective and hence bijective.

nodes.name: zeta+ surjective
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F$. Note $S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}\in\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ and $T(f)\in F_0$. We have \begin{align*} \zeta^+(S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}, T(f)) &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} T(f) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} f \\ &= f. \end{align*} Thus, $\zeta^+$ is surjective.

nodes.name: zeta+ injective
nodes.statement: Suppose $\zeta^+(A_1,f_1)=\zeta^+(A_2,f_2)$. Thus, $A_1f_1=A_2f_2$, so that $(A_2^{-1}A_1)f_1=f_2$. Since $f_1$ and $f_2$ are Parseval, then Lemma \ref{UnitaryParseval} implies that $A_2^{-1}A_1$ is unitary. Thus, \[ (A_2^{-1}A_1)(A_2^{-1}A_1)^* = A_2^{-1}A_1A_1^*(A_2^{-1})^* = I. \] Since $A_2^{-1}$ and $A_1$ are positive and hence self-adjoint, then \begin{align*} A_2^{-1}A_1A_1A_2^{-1} &= I. \\ A_1^2 &= A_2^2. \end{align*} Since $A_1$ and $A_2$ are positive, then the unique principal square roots of $A_1^2$ and $A_2^2$ are precisely $A_1$ and $A_2$ respectively. Thus, we have $A_1=A_2$. This implies $A_2^{-1}A_1=I$, so that $f_1=f_2$. That is, $(A_1,f_1)=(A_2,f_2)$. Thus, $\zeta^+$ is injective and hence bijective.
nodes.statement_short: Unitary lemma plus uniqueness of positive square roots

nodes.name: Continuity
nodes.statement: Finally, we prove $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are both continuous: Since $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are both restrictions of the map $\zeta_*:\operatorname{GL}(H)\times F_0\mapsto F$, then it suffices to show $\zeta_*$ is continuous. Let $\{(A_n,f_n)\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of points in $\operatorname{GL}(H)\times F_0$., and suppose $(A_n,f_n)\rightarrow (A,f)$. This means $A_n\rightarrow A$ and $f_n\rightarrow f$. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then, there exists $N_1\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N_1$ implies \[ \|A_n-A\|_H,\|f_n-f\|_J <\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}. \] Since $A_n\rightarrow A$, then there exists $N_2\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N_2$ implies $\|A_n\|_H<2\|A\|_H$. Assume $n>\max\{N_1,N_2\}$. Then, we have \begin{align*} \|\zeta_*(A_n,f_n)-\zeta_*(A,f)\|_J &= \|A_nf_n-Af\|_J \\ &= \|A_nf_n-A_nf+A_nf-Af\|_J \\ &\leq \|A_nf_n-A_nf\|_J+\|A_nf-Af\|_J \\ &= \sup_{x\in X} \|A_n(f_n-f)(x)\|_H+\sup_{x\in X} \|(A_n-A)f(x)\|_H \\ &\leq \|A_n\|_H \sup_{x\in X}\|(f_n-f)(x)\|_H + \|A_n-A\|_H\sup_{x\in X}\|f(x)\|_H \\ &= \|A_n\|_H\|f_n-f\|_J+\|A_n-A\|_H\|f\|_J \\ &< 2\|A\|_H\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}\right)+\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}\right)\|f\|_J \\ &= \varepsilon. \end{align*} Ergo, $\zeta_*$ and thus $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are continuous.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: Since $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are both restrictions of the map $\zeta_*:\operatorname{GL}(H)\times F_0\mapsto F$, then it suffices to show $\zeta_*$ is continuous.

nodes.name: Sequence setup
nodes.statement: Let $\{(A_n,f_n)\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of points in $\operatorname{GL}(H)\times F_0$., and suppose $(A_n,f_n)\rightarrow (A,f)$. This means $A_n\rightarrow A$ and $f_n\rightarrow f$. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then, there exists $N_1\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N_1$ implies \[ \|A_n-A\|_H,\|f_n-f\|_J <\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}. \]

nodes.name: Uniform bound
nodes.statement: Since $A_n\rightarrow A$, then there exists $N_2\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N_2$ implies $\|A_n\|_H<2\|A\|_H$.

nodes.name: Estimate
nodes.statement: Assume $n>\max\{N_1,N_2\}$. Then, we have \begin{align*} \|\zeta_*(A_n,f_n)-\zeta_*(A,f)\|_J &= \|A_nf_n-Af\|_J \\ &= \|A_nf_n-A_nf+A_nf-Af\|_J \\ &\leq \|A_nf_n-A_nf\|_J+\|A_nf-Af\|_J \\ &= \sup_{x\in X} \|A_n(f_n-f)(x)\|_H+\sup_{x\in X} \|(A_n-A)f(x)\|_H \\ &\leq \|A_n\|_H \sup_{x\in X}\|(f_n-f)(x)\|_H + \|A_n-A\|_H\sup_{x\in X}\|f(x)\|_H \\ &= \|A_n\|_H\|f_n-f\|_J+\|A_n-A\|_H\|f\|_J \\ &< 2\|A\|_H\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}\right)+\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}\right)\|f\|_J \\ &= \varepsilon. \end{align*} Ergo, $\zeta_*$ and thus $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are continuous.

nodes.name: Orbit indexing
nodes.statement: Because $\zeta:\operatorname{GL}(H)\times\overline{F}_0\mapsto F$ is a bijection, the orbit space $F/\operatorname{GL}(H)$ is in one-one correspondence with $\overline{F}_0$. In other words, the transversal $\overline{F}_0$ of unitarily inequivalent Parseval frames indexes the orbits in $F$ induced by invertible linear transformations.

nodes.name: Unique representation
nodes.statement: In particular, because $\zeta$ is invertible, we have that $$F = \operatorname{GL}(H)\overline{F}_0,$$ with every frame having a unique representation in $\operatorname{GL}(H)\overline{F}_0$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Recalling the relationship between $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ and $\operatorname{GL}(H)$, the following corollary completes this line of thought.

nodes.name: Surjective
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\operatorname{GL}(H)$. Then, $Af_{10}\in F_1$. By Corollary \ref{Identity}, we have \begin{align*} Af_{10} &= \zeta(\pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(Af_{10})), \pi_2(\zeta^{-1}(Af_{10}))) \\ &= \zeta(\theta(Af_{10})), f_{10}) \\ &= \theta(Af_{10})f_{10}. \end{align*} But since $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ acts regularly on $F_1$ (by Lemma \ref{Regular}), then $\theta(Af_{10})=A$. Ergo, $\theta$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity via identity corollary and regularity

nodes.name: Injective
nodes.statement: Suppose $\theta(f_1) = \theta(f_2)$. As above, $f_1$ and $f_2$ have the unique factorizations $f_1=\theta(f_1)f_{10}$ and $f_2=\theta(f_2)f_{10}$. But since $\theta(f_1)=\theta(f_2)$, then \[ f_1 = \theta(f_1)f_{10} = \theta(f_2)f_{10} = f_2. \] Thus, $\theta$ is injective.

nodes.name: Bijection
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{theta}, $\theta$ is bijective. The identity map is obviously bijective. Thus, the map \[ (f_1,f_0)\rightarrow (\theta(f_1), f_0) \] is a bijection from $F_1\times\overline{F}_0$ to $\operatorname{GL}(H)\times\overline{F}_0$. By Theorem \ref{zeta}, $\zeta$ is bijective. Ergo, $\theta_*$ is a bijection.

nodes.name: Inverse
nodes.statement: To verify that the expression $\theta_*^{-1}$ is indeed the inverse of $\theta_*$, let $f\in F$ and consider \begin{align*} \theta_*(\theta_*^{-1}(f)) &= \zeta(\theta(T_1(f)), \sigma\circ T(f)) \\ &= \zeta[\pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}(\pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}(f)f_{10}), \sigma\circ T(f)] \\ &= \zeta(\pi_1\zeta^{-1}(f), \sigma\circ T(f)) \\ &= \pi_1(\zeta(f))\sigma(T(f)) \\ &= f. \end{align*} The reverse composition proceeds similarly.

nodes.name: Component continuity
nodes.statement: Suppose $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous. Then, $\theta = \pi_1\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous. By Theorem \ref{zeta}, $\zeta$ is continuous. Thus, $\theta_*(f_1,f_0) = \zeta(\theta(f_1), f_0)$ is continuous Since $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous, then $T_1(f) = \pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f))f_{10}$ and $\sigma\circ T = \pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}$ are continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of $\theta_*$, $T_1$ and $\sigma\circ T$ from that of $\zeta^{-1}$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Thus, $\theta_*^{-1} = (T_1, \sigma\circ T)$ is continuous. Ergo, $\theta_*$ is a homeomorphism. Since $F$ is homeomorphic to the product space $F_1\times\overline{F}_0$ (via $\theta_*^{-1}$), then $F$ is trivially a fiber bundle as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: $\theta_*$ is a homeomorphism, so $F$ is a product bundle

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of frames in $F$ and $f\in F$ such that $f_n\rightarrow f$ in $J_1$. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then, there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N$ implies $\|f_n\|_{J_1}<2\|f\|_{j_1}$ and \[ \|f_n-f\|_{J_1} < \frac{\varepsilon}{3\|f\|_{J_1}}. \]

nodes.name: Splitting
nodes.statement: Suppose $n>N$. Consider any $\phi\in H$. We have \begin{align*} \|S(f_n)\phi-S(f)\phi\|_H &= \left\|\int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f_n(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ &= \left\|\int_X \brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f_n(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right. \\ & \qquad + \left.\int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ &= \left\|\int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H [f_n(x)-f(x)]\,d\mu(x) + \int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)-f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ & \leq \int_X \|\phi\|_H\|f_n(x)\|_H\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H\,d\mu(x) \\ & \qquad + \int_X\|\phi\|_H\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H\|f\|_H\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \|\phi\|\int_X \|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H (\|f_n(x)\|_H+\|f(x)\|_H)\,d\mu(x). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Hoelder bound
nodes.statement: By H\"{o}lder's Inequality, we have \begin{align*} \|S(f_n)\phi-S(f)\phi\|_H &\leq \|\phi\|_H\int_X\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H\,d\mu(x)\int_X(\|f_n(x)\|_H+\|f(x)\|_H)\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \|\phi\|_H\|f_n-f\|_{J_1}(\|f_n\|_{J_1}+\|f\|_{J_1}) \\ &< 3\|f\|_{J_1}\|f_n-f\|_{J_1}\|\phi\|_H \\ &< \varepsilon \|\phi\|_H. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Since this holds for all $\phi\in H$, then $\|S(f_n)-S(f)\|_H<\varepsilon$. Ergo, $S(f_n)\rightarrow S(f)$, and hence $S$ is continuous.

nodes.name: Apply SCont
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of frames in $F$ and $f\in F$ such that $f_n\rightarrow f$ in $J_1$. By Lemma \ref{SCont}, $S(f_n)\rightarrow S(f)$.

nodes.name: Inverse square root
nodes.statement: Since the map sending an operator in $\operatorname{GL}(H)$ to its inverse and the map sending an operator in $\operatorname{GL}^+(H)$ to its principal square root are both continuous in the operator norm, then $S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\rightarrow S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then, there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N$ implies $\|f_n\|_{J_1}<2\|f\|_{J_1}$ and \[ \|f-f_n\|_{J_1},\|S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H < \delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|f\|_{J_1}+\|S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H}. \]

nodes.name: Factorization
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F_0$. Then, $f_0$ has the unique factorization $f = U(f)\sigma(f)$. For any $\phi\in H$ and for all $x\in X$, we have \[ \brak{\phi, f(x)}_H = \brak{\phi, U(f)\sigma(f)(x)}_H = \brak{U(f)^*\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H. \]

nodes.name: Formula for U
nodes.statement: Letting $V_g$ and $V_g^*$ denote the analysis and synthesis operators of a frame $g\in F$, we have \[ V_f\phi = V_{\sigma(f)}U(f)^*\phi, \] or simply $V_f = V_{\sigma(f)}U(f)^*$. Thus, $V_fU(f) = V_{\sigma(f)}$, and hence $V_f^*V_fU(f) = V_f^*V_{\sigma(f)}$. But since $f$ is Parseval, then $V_f^*V_f = S(f)=I$ so that \[ U(f) = V_f^* V_{\sigma(f)}. \] Thus, for all $\phi\in H$, we have \begin{equation} U(f)\phi = \int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: To show $U$ is continuous, let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of frames in $F_0$ and $f\in F_0$ with $f_n\rightarrow f$ in $J_1$. Since $\sigma$ is continuous, then $\sigma(f_n)\rightarrow\sigma(f)$. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then, there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N$ implies $\|f_n\|_{J_1}<2\|f\|_{J_1}$ and \[ \|f_n-f\|_{J_1}, \|\sigma(f_n)-\sigma(f)\|_{J_1} < \delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{\|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1}+2\|f\|_{J_1}}. \]

nodes.name: Estimate
nodes.statement: Suppose $n>N$. Let $\phi\in H$. By manipulations similar to those used in the proof of Lemma \ref{SCont} (including the Triangle Inequality, Cauchy-Schwartz Inequality, and H\"{o}lder's Inequality), we have \begin{align*} \|U(f_n)\phi-U(f)\phi\|_H &= \left\|\int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f_n)(x)}_H f_n(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ &\leq \|\phi\|_H \|\sigma(f_n)-\sigma(f)\|_{J_1}\|f_n\|_{J_1} + \|\phi\|_H \|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1} \|f_n-f\|_{J_1} \\ &< \|\phi\|_H \delta 2\|f\|_{J_1} + \|\phi\|_H \|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1} \delta \\ &= (2\|f\|_{J_1}+\|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1})\delta \|\phi\|_H \\ &= \varepsilon \|\phi\|_H. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Estimate as in the proof for $S$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Since this holds for all $\phi\in H$, then $\|U(f_n)-U(f)\|_H < \varepsilon$. Ergo, $U(f_n)\rightarrow U(f)$, and hence $U$ is continuous.

nodes.name: Recall
nodes.statement: Recall that $\zeta^{-1}$ is given by \[ \zeta^{-1}(f) = (S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(f), \sigma\circ T(f)). \]

nodes.name: Continuity
nodes.statement: By Lemmas \ref{SCont}-\ref{UCont}, the maps $S$, $T$, and $U$ are continuous in $J_1$. Moreover, $\sigma$ and the square root function are continuous as well. Therefore, $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{IfzetaCont}, $F$ is a fiber bundle as claimed.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: A special case occurs when $\mu$ is a finite measure on $X$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: In this case, convergence in $J=L^\infty(X,H)$ implies convergence in $J_1=L^1(X,H)$. We therefore have the following corollary.
